LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA

ABOUT

Gaia — iNaturalist rebrand and app

Turning noticing into a way of

caring for the living world.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

Gaia began as a personal exploration of two things I love: the outdoors and the community of people who share what they find there. I rebranded and redesigned iNaturalist, the world’s largest biodiversity platform, to turn a tool built for experts into an open invitation for anyone curious about nature.

I scaled one identity into a complete visual system of logotype, color, typography, and icons, then extended the system across print, out of home, digital, and interactive pieces. I worked alone at every stage, from strategy and identity to a working iOS app I built in SwiftUI.

/ INDUSTRY

Nature

/ SCOPE

Visual Identity, UX/UI, Strategy

/ CREDITS

Client: Self-Initiated Proposal

Designer: Micah Hoang

/ YEAR

2026

The Insight

iNaturalist lets people photograph an organism, receive an AI-assisted identification, and contribute research-grade data used by scientists to combat a global extinction crisis.

Strategy

Three goals shape every decision: increase access, increase motivation, increase meaning. Across the arc from wonder to stewardship, noticing becomes a habit of care.

iNaturalist asks you to be a naturalist first. For most people, that is a title they never claim. Gaia preserves the same scientific rigor while opening the platform to a broader audience.

Visual Identity

The mark grows from a branching, living form. Inspired by Werner's Nomenclature of Colours, the palette draws from moss, paper, soil, and sky. New Spirit carries the expressive moments; Neue Haas Unica handles every working word.

Brand in the World

Gaia reaches people where they already meet the living world: botanical gardens, museums, trailheads, and community bioblitzes.

Interface

A custom icon system pairs with botanical illustrations drawn in a nineteenth-century naturalist style, keeping the interface scientific in structure and warm in tone.

The map invites before it asks. Plain language and an obvious way in lower the barrier to a first observation.

A single observation becomes part of something shared, joining a community record that gives each find meaning beyond the moment.

Every find is met with a small moment of pride, turning a single observation into a reason to look again.

Designed to Ship

The work was pressure-tested against real constraints, not presented only as static screens. Core interactions, including map clustering, the bottom sheet, the observation flow, and the detail tabs, were built in SwiftUI, with a live prototype running on Mapbox GL. Midjourney supported directed image generation, while Claude Code accelerated prototype testing and token management.

simon-schuster.text:
Simon & Schuster — rebrand concept
The last independent,
made to look like it.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

In 2022, the Justice Department blocked Penguin Random House from buying Simon & Schuster, preserving one of the last independently owned Big Five publishers. Most coverage framed the ruling as a near miss, but I saw a positioning opportunity: independence as the asset, not the consolation prize.

I grounded this self-initiated rebrand in real market data and focused my work on the visual result: an identity system spanning print, event design, digital, and social media.

/ INDUSTRY

Literature

/ SCOPE

Brand Strategy, Visual Identity, Editorial

/ CREDITS

Client: Self-Initiated Proposal

Designer: Micah Hoang

/ YEAR

2024

/ RECOGNITION

Indigo Design Award: Gold

Fonts in Use: Feature

DNA Paris: Winner

Background

Five conglomerates control trade publishing. S&S is the smallest, and after the block, the only one whose independence is now its defining trait. Founded in 1924, it publishes 2,000 titles a year across more than 50 imprints. Scale and independence usually read as separate stories. I built the brand where they meet.

Statistics & Insights

I started where the conglomerates weren't looking.  Both pointed to the same move. The strategy followed the data.

Strategy

An antitrust block looks like a loss. I made it the advantage no competitor can copy, because the others are owned. The manifesto commits S&S to emerging authors, transparent acquisition, and mentorship as proof of the position.

Logomark

I merged the ampersand with an “S” so one mark could carry more than 50 imprints without redrawing any. Set in PP Editorial New, it reads first as a publisher's mark. The system works three ways: standalone, locked to type, and as a stamp. Paired with an author's signature, it gives each collaboration its own lockup.

Guidelines
‹
›

A 65-page book to govern 2,000 titles a year across dozens of imprints. These spreads show the load-bearing rules: the imprint lockup, the signature-collaboration system, the grid that holds both. The rest of the book just applies them.

Brand Architecture

Three divisions, more than 50 imprints. I paired the new wordmark with each imprint logo instead of replacing it, so every imprint retains its identity while still reading as part of one house. The hardest cases were imprints with strong marks of their own. Each lockup had to defer to those marks while still signaling the parent brand.

Print
Digital

I built the storefront to beat the marketplaces on the one axis they can't match: curation. Independence only counts if a reader feels it while browsing, so the experience leads with editorial spotlights for small and diverse authors.

Event

I launched a new Children's imprint, Voyager, to stress-test the architecture. It uses the lockup rule with no exceptions. 

Collaborations

I designed a campaign with the ALA's Office for Intellectual Freedom that offered historically banned books at 50% off. Each release received a custom poster that blended the title's identity with the institutional mark. A publisher built on independence should speak loudly for the books others tried to remove.

ABOUT

Peak Energy & GM — partnership motion design
Announcing a new
era of energy.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

Peak Energy builds sodium-ion batteries, a domestic alternative to lithium and a technology at the center of the next energy shift. This brand film announced the company's partnership with General Motors. It places sodium-ion on the timeline of human energy and frames Peak Energy as a leader in the next phase of power.

I led the central animation sequence, developing the storyboards, directing the visual language, and building a precise line-based system that could carry both abstract concepts and product detail.

/ INDUSTRY

Technology

/ SCOPE

2D Motion, 3D Motion, Social Media

/ CREDITS

Client: Peak Energy

Featured Partner: General Motors

Creative Lead: Micah Hoang

2D Animation & Compositing: Micah Hoang

3D Animation: Jonathan Kusnadi, Wesley Ching

Sound & VO: Peak Energy Team

/ YEAR

2026

The Brief

Sodium-ion is an emerging category, and the film had to make it feel like the obvious next step. The brief was to build public and investor confidence in the technology and position Peak Energy at the frontier of rising power demands from AI and automation.

My Role

I led the central sequence from storyboard pitches through client reviews and visual development. Two 3D motion designers and I built out the scenes from there; I handled compositing and timed the edit to the voiceover.

The Tension

The film had to move between two registers: abstract ideas such as grid stability and energy density, and a technically accurate view of the battery itself. Both had to live within the same sleek, line-based world and transition smoothly between scales.

The Solution

We chose a line-based language to signal precision and engineering. To keep it from feeling cold, I layered in subtle grain, film chatter, and shake, tying the film to the older eras of energy it traces and giving the technical work some character.

The team modeled in Blender and C4D with Redshift toon shaders. I composited those passes with hand-built animation in After Effects, using a consistent stroke treatment so the conceptual sequences could resolve into the exploded battery view.

What Shipped

Our sequence anchors the center of the film and carries the GM reveal. Using the same system, I built the closing logo animation, which continues to serve as the signature for new posts about the partnership.

motion-connect-2025.text:
Motion Connect 2025 — ArtCenter event identity
Amping up the world of
moving design.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

Motion Connect is an ArtCenter talk series bringing the motion design community together, with 2025 speakers from Apple TV, Hornet, and Brand New School.

I based the identity on 1980s arcade graphics: bitmap glow, scanlines, and the boot-up energy of a machine powering on. From those cues, I built a brand system and carried the system across the motion reel, social media, and print, so every piece reads as part of one season.

/ INDUSTRY

Education

/ SCOPE

2D Motion, 3D Motion, Social Media

/ CREDITS

Client: ArtCenter College of Design

Lead Designer: Micah Hoang

Concept Development: Allyssa Acevedo, Michelle Theodorus

/ YEAR

2025

Hype Reel

A 45-second reel introduced the speakers, showed their work, and built anticipation for the event. It opened the program once the audience was seated.

Social Media

An animated Instagram carousel translated the system into a vertical format, letting people scroll through the lineup and event details on social.

Print Assets

A printed poster and widescreen graphic brought the identity across campus, extending the moving system into static formats.

The System

One effect holds the whole identity together: a bitmap scanline and atmospheric glow run across every frame, piece of typography, and 3D form, so distinct assets read as one system. I built the pipeline to match: type modeled and animated in 3D, unified in After Effects through color and the scanline pass, then finished in Photoshop for print.

AI Workflows

Working solo for two weeks, I built every asset from scratch. AI helped close production gaps: I generated auditorium drone footage from stills without a shoot, and used Runway for lighting and motion tests before committing to full renders.

Live

At the live event, the system took over the room. An ambient loop ran as the auditorium filled, and the hype reel opened the program on the main screen.

ABOUT

National Park Playing Cards — illustration and packaging
Bestselling love letter
to the outdoors.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

National Park Playing Cards started as my tribute to U.S. national parks and grew into a business I still run, with 20,000+ decks sold. The decks sell in 220+ stores nationwide, including REI and six national park visitor centers.

I designed the full product system: cards, box, brand, and storefront. I also funded the launch on Kickstarter, built the business, and pitched retailers myself.

/ INDUSTRY

Nature

/ SCOPE

Packaging, Product

/ CREDITS

Client: Self-Initiated Proposal
Founder and Designer: Micah Hoang
Photography: Keaton Wong, Ethan Hosford

/ YEAR

2019

The Problem

Fifty-two cards. Fifty-two parks. I decided early that the deck should not just illustrate parks; it should encode them. The standard structure of suits and ranks had to carry two extra layers of meaning: region and visitation, without ever breaking as a deck you could actually play.

The System

Each suit maps to a U.S. region: diamonds to the Southwest, spades to the Northwest, clubs to the East, and hearts to the South. Card values rank the parks by popularity, from aces for the most visited down to twos for the least visited.

The jokers depict two iconic North American animals: the American black bear and American elk.

Card Craft

Minimal linework depicts the 52 most popular U.S. national parks. The face cards use filled-in circles with negative-space lines to distinguish them from the other cards.

The back of each card depicts natural elements, including the sun, moon, trees, mountains, and leaves.

Playability

The deck is engineered as a working deck, not a decorative object. The stock, finish, and registration are specified to a standard that lets the cards handle, fan, and spring well enough for card magic and sleight of hand, not just display.

Box Design

I specified silver foil pressed onto a matte uncoated box. Visitor center shelves are full of cheap, commercial decks, and I wanted this one to read as a keepsake the moment someone picks it up. The foiled National Park Service arrowhead, rendered in a retro line style, is the shelf cue that signals quality before anyone opens it.

In Retail

The cards reached more than 200 boutique retailers across 49 states, plus the visitor centers at Canyonlands, Arches, Saguaro, Mount Rainier, Shenandoah, and Zion. I placed every one of these accounts myself, cold emailing and cold calling buyers with no distributor or sales rep.

Building the Business

Driven by my love for the outdoors and U.S. national parks, I launched National Park Playing Cards in 2019 through a 30-day Kickstarter campaign that I designed, built, and ran myself. The goal was $2,500 to produce 500 decks. I raised $6,341, which let me print 1,000 decks and ship 300 to backers.

After the first run sold out, I built the direct-to-consumer business: a Shopify storefront I designed and built, plus Etsy and Amazon listings. Direct online sales were the primary revenue source in the early years. I partnered with a friend to run paid acquisition across Google, Meta, and TikTok while I owned the product, the storefront, and the brand.

As demand grew, I moved the business toward wholesale, which is where most of the revenue comes from today. I handled buyer outreach for every account myself. In 2022, REI brought the deck into its stores and told me that, at 18, I was the youngest vendor it had ever signed.

By the Numbers

ABOUT

Weaponized Innocence — editorial and advocacy design
Some childhoods are taken.

/ ABOUT THE PROJECT

Weaponized Innocence is a newsprint publication about the exploitation of children in warfare. It moves from the realities of child soldiering toward the possibility of rehabilitation, emphasizing UNICEF's role in protecting affected children and helping them rebuild their lives.

Complementing the editorial is The Pinwheel Project, an interactive bonus piece featuring pinwheels adorned with drawings by child survivors and excerpts from Emmanuel Jal and Betty Ejang. Together, the publication and pinwheel kit are built to drive advocacy and support for UNICEF's mission.

/ INDUSTRY

Human Rights

/ SCOPE

Editorial, Product

/ CREDITS

Client: Self-Initiated Proposal; Designer: Micah Hoang

/ YEAR

2024

/ RECOGNITION

Fonts in Use: Feature

Background

Child soldiers represent one of the most harrowing violations of human rights, with tens of thousands of children forced into warfare around the world. UNICEF has long fought to protect these children by securing their release, offering rehabilitation, and advocating for systemic change.

Cover

The front cover captures the chaos and horror of child soldiering, using fragmented visuals to convey the brutality of the issue. In contrast, the back cover introduces the pinwheel as a symbol of renewal and possibility.

Interior
‹
›

The interior moves from disjointed, chaotic layouts to clean, balanced spreads, mirroring a path from trauma toward recovery.

Stark infographics establish scale and context, while childlike illustrations convey the emotional toll of child soldiering. Together, they balance information with emotional impact and emphasize the transformative role of UNICEF's work.

The Pinwheel Project

The Pinwheel Project is a hands-on pinwheel-making kit designed for stakeholders and educational campaigns. Assembling the pinwheel becomes a metaphor for rebuilding a life, turning a simple act into a gesture of care and renewal.

Each pinwheel design showcases a distinctive blend of drawings by former child soldiers and rap lyrics by Emmanuel Jal, a poet and musician who survived child soldiering.

Process

A 9-column grid creates dynamic, asymmetric spreads in the first half and shifts to a clean, informational tone in the second half.

Midjourney AI was used to generate chaotic, childlike, and nightmarish drawings depicting the fear and horror of warfare and forced soldiering from a child's perspective.
